questions.question: Which of the following states shares its boundary with Bangladesh?

questions.question: The village headman during the Gupta period was commonly known as _____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gramadhyaksha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During the Gupta period, the **Gramadhyaksha** was the village headman responsible for the administration, management, and overall welfare of the village.
 
• He acted as a link between the rural population and the central administration, ensuring the smooth functioning of the governance at the village level.
 
• The Gramadhyaksha was tasked with maintaining law and order, collecting revenue, and addressing disputes within the village.
 
• This role was highly regarded during the Gupta period, as villages were considered the smallest unit of governance and the backbone of the empire’s economy.
 
• The Gramadhyaksha worked in coordination with other officials, such as the Mahattara, to ensure efficient governance and tax collection.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahattara:**

 
 
• The Mahattara was a senior village official during the Gupta period, often assisting the Gramadhyaksha in administrative duties.
 
• They were primarily responsible for advising the Gramadhyaksha on important matters related to governance and village welfare.
 
• In some cases, they also played a role in revenue collection and land management.
 
 
 
• **Uparika:**
 
 
• The Uparika was a provincial governor during the Gupta period.
 
• They were responsible for overseeing the administration of a province or region within the empire, ensuring adherence to the central government’s directives.
 
• The Uparika reported directly to the central administration and played a key role in maintaining the empire’s stability.
 
 
 
• **Amatyas:**
 
 
• The Amatyas were ministers or high-ranking officials in the Gupta administration.
 
• They were responsible for advising the king on matters of state and assisting in the governance of the empire.
 
• Amatyas often held specialized portfolios, such as finance, defense, or justice, and played a critical role in policy formulation and implementation.

questions.question: What was the major demographic feature of India at the time of independence?

options.text: High death rate and infant mortality

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**High death rate and infant mortality**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• At the time of independence in 1947, India had a very high **death rate** and **infant mortality rate**, primarily due to lack of healthcare facilities, malnutrition, and widespread diseases.
 
• The **infant mortality rate** was alarmingly high, with a significant percentage of children not surviving beyond their first year of life.
 
• India faced widespread epidemics such as cholera, malaria, and tuberculosis, which further contributed to the high death rate.
 
• Limited access to medical care and poor sanitation were major contributors to the demographic challenges at the time.
 
• The life expectancy during independence was also very low, around **32 years**, due to the high prevalence of diseases and poor living conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **High life expectancy**

 
 
• Life expectancy refers to the average number of years a person is expected to live based on current mortality trends.
 
• At the time of independence, India's life expectancy was extremely low (around 32 years), so this option is incorrect.
 
• Over the years, improvements in healthcare, nutrition, and sanitation have significantly increased life expectancy in India, which is now over 70 years.
 
 
 
• **Aging population**
 
 
• An aging population refers to a demographic trend where the proportion of elderly people in the population increases.
 
• At independence, India had a predominantly young population, with a high birth rate and a low life expectancy, making this option incorrect.
 
• Currently, India still has a young population, but an aging population is expected to emerge as a concern in the future.
 
 
 
• **Low birth rate**
 
 
• Birth rate refers to the number of live births per thousand people in a year.
 
• At the time of independence, India had a very high birth rate, not a low one, due to cultural and societal norms, making this option incorrect.
 
• In recent decades, the birth rate has declined due to family planning initiatives and increased awareness.

• It is widely used in traditional medicine for its potential health benefits, including improving digestion, reducing inflammation, and managing blood sugar levels.
 
• Fenugreek seeds have a distinct aroma and are used in various cuisines worldwide, particularly in Indian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean dishes.

questions.question: The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1953**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed by the Government of India in **January 1953**.
 
• The commission was headed by **Kalelkar**, hence it is also referred to as the Kalelkar Commission.
 
• Its primary objective was to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes in India and recommend measures to improve their status.
 
• The commission submitted its report in **1955**, but the report was not implemented due to various challenges and disagreements regarding the criteria for identifying backward classes.
 
• The Kalelkar Commission is significant as it was the first attempt by the Indian government to address issues of social and educational backwardness.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)**

 
 
• National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) in India, is a constitutional body that safeguards the rights and monitors the development of socially and educationally disadvantaged groups (OBCs).
 
• It examines grievances, evaluates welfare measures, and advises the government on socio-economic development, holding constitutional status since the 102nd Amendment in 2018 under Article 338B, evolving from its earlier statutory form established in 1993.

questions.question: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act set limits on the fiscal deficit and public debt. What was the fiscal deficit target under the original FRBM Act by 2008-09?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**3% of GDP**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act was enacted in **2003** to institutionalize financial discipline and reduce India’s fiscal deficit.
 
• Under the original FRBM Act, the fiscal deficit target was set at **3% of GDP** by **2008-09**.
 
• The FRBM Act aimed to ensure **long-term macroeconomic stability** and improve fiscal management by reducing government borrowing and debt levels.
 
• The Act required the government to submit an annual **Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement** to Parliament, outlining plans to meet fiscal targets.
 
• While the FRBM Act mandated fiscal consolidation, compliance faced challenges due to economic downturns and external pressures such as the global financial crisis of **2008**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act**

 
 
• The FRBM Act is a landmark legislation aimed at ensuring fiscal prudence and reducing government debt.
 
• It introduced measures to improve transparency in India’s fiscal policy and impose fiscal discipline on the government.
 
• Amendments to the FRBM Act have been introduced over the years to accommodate changing economic realities, including provisions for exceptional circumstances like national security or severe economic downturns.
 
 
 
• Zero deficit
 
 
• A zero fiscal deficit implies that government expenditure matches revenue exactly, without borrowing. While theoretically desirable, it is impractical for a growing economy like India, which requires borrowing for infrastructure and development projects.
 
• The FRBM Act did not mandate a zero deficit but aimed to reduce the deficit to sustainable levels.

questions.question: Which two researchers independently suggested that acid-base reactions could be thought of as proton-transfer reactions for the first time, in 1923?

options.text: Guillaume F Rouelle and Humphry Davy
Gilbert N Lewis and SPL Sorensen
JN Brønsted and Thomas M Lowry

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**JN Brønsted and Thomas M Lowry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted** (Denmark) and **Thomas Martin Lowry** (England) independently proposed the concept of acid-base reactions as proton transfer reactions in 1923.
 
• The **Brønsted-Lowry theory** defines acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
 
• This theory expanded the understanding of acid-base chemistry beyond the Arrhenius definition, accommodating reactions in non-aqueous solvents.
 
• Their work laid the foundation for modern acid-base chemistry and is widely applicable in chemical, biological, and industrial processes.
 
• The Brønsted-Lowry model is particularly significant because it explains acid-base behavior in the absence of water, making it more versatile than earlier models.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Guillaume F. Rouelle and Humphry Davy:**

 
 
• Guillaume F. Rouelle was a French chemist who introduced the concept of acids and their reactions in the 18th century, but he did not develop a proton-transfer model.
 
• Humphry Davy (1778-1829) was a British chemist who studied the chemical properties of acids and bases, suggesting that their action was related to their composition but did not propose the proton-transfer model.
 
 
 
• **Svante Arrhenius and Peter Waage:**
 
 
• Svante Arrhenius proposed the Arrhenius definition of acids and bases in 1884, stating that acids produce H⁺ ions in water and bases produce OH−.
 
• Peter Waage, along with Cato Guldberg, formulated the Law of Mass Action in 1864, which describes chemical equilibrium but does not focus on acid-base proton transfer.
 
 
 
• **Gilbert N Lewis and S.P.L. Sørensen:**
 
 
• Gilbert N. Lewis proposed the Lewis definition of acids and bases in 1923, identifying acids as electron pair acceptors and bases as electron pair donors.
 
• S.P.L. Sørensen was a Danish chemist who introduced the pH scale in 1909, facilitating the measurement of acidity but did not propose a proton-transfer model.

questions.question: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021, is related to which of the following?

options.text: Creation of a National Judicial Commission
Powers of state governments to identify OBCs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Powers of state governments to identify OBCs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021, restored the **power of states and union territories to identify and notify Other Backward Classes (OBCs)** for their respective regions.
 
• This amendment modified Article 342A, empowering states to prepare their own list of OBCs distinct from the central list.
 
• The amendment was necessitated after the Supreme Court’s judgment in the Maratha quota case (2021), which limited the powers of states to notify OBCs.
 
• It allows states to provide reservations for OBCs in jobs and educational institutions based on regional requirements.
 
• The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act ensures decentralization and caters to the socio-economic needs of backward classes at the state level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Creation of a National Judicial Commission**

 
 
• The National Judicial Commission has been proposed in the past as a mechanism for judicial appointments and oversight.
 
• It aims to replace the collegium system of appointing judges to the higher judiciary.
 
• The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act (2014) sought to establish the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), but it was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015, citing violation of judicial independence.
 
 
 
• **GST Reforms**
 
 
• GST reforms pertain to the Goods and Services Tax (GST), a comprehensive indirect tax regime introduced in India in 2017.
 
• GST reforms focus on simplifying tax compliance, reducing tax evasion, and addressing issues like compensation to states and rate rationalization.
 
• While GST reforms are significant, they are unrelated to the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act.
 
 
 
• **Women’s Reservation**
 
 
• Women’s reservation refers to the legislative proposal to reserve seats for women in Parliament and state legislatures.
 
• The Women’s Reservation Bill seeks to reserve 33% of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.
 
• While this is an important initiative, it is not connected to the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act.

questions.question: Which of the following courts is known as the 'Guardian of the Constitution' in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Supreme Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Supreme Court of India is known as the **'Guardian of the Constitution'** because it ensures the enforcement and protection of the fundamental rights of citizens.
 
• It has the authority to interpret the Constitution and resolve disputes between the Union and States or among States themselves.
 
• Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court guarantees the right to constitutional remedies, allowing individuals to approach the court directly in case of violation of their fundamental rights.
 
• The Supreme Court is vested with the power of judicial review, which enables it to strike down any law or executive action that it deems unconstitutional.
 
• It is the apex judicial authority in India, and its decisions are binding on all other courts in the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **District Court**

 
 
• District Courts are subordinate courts that deal with civil and criminal cases at the district level.
 
• They function under the supervision of the High Court of the respective state.
 
• While they play an important role in the justice delivery system, they do not have constitutional authority like the Supreme Court.
 
 
 
• **High Court**
 
 
• High Courts are the highest judicial bodies at the state level and handle civil, criminal, and constitutional matters within their jurisdiction.
 
• They also have the power of judicial review but are subordinate to the Supreme Court.
 
• High Courts can interpret the Constitution but cannot act as the ultimate guardian of constitutional provisions like the Supreme Court.
 
 
 
• **Lok Adalat**
 
 
• Lok Adalat is a system of alternative dispute resolution in India aimed at resolving disputes outside the formal judicial process.
 
• It is governed by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and is primarily used for settling civil disputes and minor criminal cases.
 
• While it promotes speedy and amicable settlements, it does not have constitutional authority or the power to interpret the Constitution.

questions.question: Transition elements are generally found in which block of the periodic table?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**d-block**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Transition elements are found in the **d-block** of the periodic table, which includes elements from groups 3 to 12.
 
• These elements are characterized by the progressive filling of the d-orbitals of their atoms.
 
• The d-block elements are also referred to as transition metals and include elements such as iron (Fe), copper (Cu), and chromium (Cr).
 
• They exhibit unique properties such as variable oxidation states, the formation of colored compounds, and the ability to form complexes.
 
• The d-block elements play a crucial role in industries due to their catalytic properties and their application in alloys, electronics, and other fields.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **s-block:**

 
 
• The s-block elements are found in groups 1 and 2 of the periodic table, including alkali metals (e.g., sodium, potassium) and alkaline earth metals (e.g., magnesium, calcium).
 
• Their outermost electrons occupy the s-orbital, and they typically exhibit a single oxidation state.
 
• These elements are highly reactive, especially with water and oxygen, and are good conductors of heat and electricity.
 
 
 
• **p-block:**
 
 
• The p-block elements are located in groups 13 to 18 of the periodic table.
 
• These include non-metals (e.g., oxygen, nitrogen), metalloids (e.g., boron, silicon), and some metals (e.g., aluminum, lead).
 
• Their outermost electrons occupy the p-orbitals, and they show a wide range of chemical and physical properties.
 
• They are involved in important industrial and biological processes, such as photosynthesis and the production of fertilizers.
 
 
 
• **f-block:**
 
 
• The f-block elements are the lanthanides and actinides, found below the main body of the periodic table.
 
• They are characterized by the filling of the 4f and 5f orbitals, respectively.
 
• These elements include rare earth metals and radioactive elements like uranium and thorium.
 
• f-block elements are used in advanced technologies, such as nuclear energy production and the development of superconductors.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation EBCDIC stand for?

• **EBCDIC** stands for **Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code**, which is an 8-bit character encoding system.
 
• It was developed by IBM in 1963-64 for use with its mainframe and midrange computer systems.
 
• EBCDIC is used for representing alphanumeric characters in binary form, primarily in IBM-based systems.
 
• It supports 256 characters, including letters, numbers, special characters, and control characters.
 
• EBCDIC is less commonly used today as most systems have transitioned to ASCII and Unicode standards, but it is still in use in legacy IBM systems.

• **Importance of EBCDIC:**

 
 
• EBCDIC played a significant role in early computing history, particularly for IBM systems.
 
• It differs from ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) in terms of design and encoding structure.
 
• While ASCII became the dominant character encoding, EBCDIC remains relevant in certain IBM mainframe environments.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a component of globalisation in India's economic reforms?

• Promoting "local-only trade" is contrary to the fundamental essence of globalization, which emphasizes international trade and the free movement of goods, services, and investments across borders.
 
• The reforms under globalization included encouraging foreign direct investment (FDI), liberalizing imports, and allowing foreign technology to foster competition and economic growth in India.

• Examples include the entry of global automobile companies and advancements in telecommunications and IT sectors.
 
 
 
• **Encouraging foreign direct investment (FDI)**:
 
 
• FDI played a pivotal role in the globalization process by bringing in foreign capital, boosting industrial growth, and generating employment opportunities.
 
• India opened up several sectors for FDI, including manufacturing, IT, retail, and infrastructure.
 
• FDI also facilitated the integration of Indian companies into global supply chains, enhancing their competitiveness.
 
 
 
• **Liberalizing imports**:
 
 
• Reducing trade barriers such as tariffs, duties, and quotas was a critical step in promoting globalization.
 
• Liberalizing imports allowed Indian consumers to access a variety of high-quality goods at competitive prices.
 
• This measure also encouraged domestic industries to improve their efficiency and quality to compete globally.

questions.question: The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, aims to:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**limit global temperature rise**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Paris Agreement, adopted in December 2015, is a landmark international treaty under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) designed to combat climate change and its adverse effects globally.
 
• The primary goal of the Paris Agreement is to limit the global average temperature increase to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the rise to 1.5°C.
 
• The agreement emphasizes the importance of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, with countries committing to implement Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and to enhance their climate action plans over time.
 
• It also focuses on strengthening resilience to climate impacts, promoting sustainable development, and providing financial support to developing nations for climate action.
 
• The Paris Agreement establishes a universal framework, recognizing the differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities of developed and developing countries in addressing climate change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Halt desertification:**

 
 
• Desertification refers to the degradation of land in arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid areas due to factors such as climatic variations and human activities.
 
• While combating desertification is an important environmental goal under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), it is not the primary focus of the Paris Agreement.
 
• Efforts to address desertification often involve sustainable land management practices, afforestation, and soil conservation techniques.
 
 
 
• **Eliminate air pollution:**
 
 
• Air pollution refers to the presence of harmful substances, such as particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, in the atmosphere.
 
• While reducing greenhouse gas emissions indirectly helps improve air quality, the Paris Agreement does not specifically aim to eliminate air pollution.
 
• Air pollution is primarily addressed through national policies, regulations, and programs like the World Health Organization’s air quality guidelines.
 
 
 
• **Promote water conservation:**
 
 
• Water conservation involves the sustainable management and use of water resources to ensure availability for future generations.
 
• Although water conservation is a critical environmental priority, it is not a direct objective of the Paris Agreement.
 
• Water conservation is often addressed through national and regional initiatives, such as watershed management, efficient irrigation practices, and rainwater harvesting.

questions.question: Slump is a type of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**landslide**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Slump** is a type of landslide that involves the downward and outward movement of a mass of rock, earth, or debris along a curved surface.
 
• In a slump, the displaced material typically rotates as it moves, creating a concave upward slide surface.
 
• Slumps are often triggered by factors such as **heavy rainfall, earthquakes, or human activities** like deforestation and construction.
 
• They are commonly observed in areas with loose, unconsolidated soils and steep slopes.
 
• Slumps are considered a type of mass wasting, which is the downslope movement of soil and rock under the influence of gravity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rock Fall:**

 
 
• A rock fall occurs when individual rocks or boulders detach from a steep slope or cliff and fall freely through the air.
 
• Rock falls are typically caused by weathering, freeze-thaw cycles, or seismic activity, which weaken the rock over time.
 
• They are most common in mountainous or rocky terrains and can pose significant hazards to infrastructure and human life in such areas.
 
 
 
• **Weathering:**
 
 
• Weathering is the process of breaking down rocks and minerals at the Earth’s surface into smaller particles through physical, chemical, or biological means.
 
• Unlike a landslide, weathering does not involve the movement of material downslope.
 
• Types of weathering include physical weathering (e.g., freeze-thaw cycles), chemical weathering (e.g., dissolution of minerals), and biological weathering (e.g., roots breaking rocks).
 
 
 
• **Erosion:**
 
 
• Erosion refers to the removal and transportation of soil, rock, and other surface materials by natural agents like water, wind, ice, or gravity.
 
• Unlike a landslide, erosion is a gradual process that occurs over an extended period of time.
 
• Common examples of erosion include riverbank erosion, coastal erosion, and wind erosion in arid regions.

questions.question: What was Gandhi’s view about the relation between means and ends in Satyagraha?

options.text: Only ends matter, not the means.
Violence is necessary for pure ends.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pure ends require pure means**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gandhi firmly believed in the principle of **ahimsa (non-violence)** as a means to achieve truth and justice in society.
 
• He emphasized that **means and ends are interconnected**; impure means would inevitably corrupt the purity of the end.
 
• The philosophy of Satyagraha highlights that **pure and ethical means** are essential for achieving righteous and ethical outcomes.
 
• Gandhi’s belief in the moral integrity of means was rooted in his spiritual and philosophical understanding of truth as the ultimate goal.
 
• He argued that adopting violent or unethical means to achieve noble ends would undermine the moral foundation of the goal itself.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Only ends matter, not the means**

 
 
• Gandhi rejected the idea that only the end result mattered, as he believed that **unethical or immoral means** would compromise the value of the outcome.
 
• This approach is contrary to Gandhi’s principle of Satyagraha, where purity of means is as important as the ends.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: The ends justify the means**
 
 
• This concept, often associated with Machiavellian philosophy, suggests that any means, even unethical ones, are acceptable if they lead to a desired goal.
 
• Gandhi strongly opposed this idea, asserting that moral corruption in the means would lead to a morally flawed end.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Violence is necessary for pure ends**
 
 
• This view contradicts Gandhi's principle of **non-violence (ahimsa)**, which he considered fundamental to achieving truth and justice.
 
• Gandhi believed that the use of violence would perpetuate a cycle of hatred and suffering, which is incompatible with achieving pure and noble ends.

questions.question: When was the Mines Act enacted in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1952**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Mines Act, 1952, was enacted by the Government of India to regulate the working conditions in mines and ensure the safety, health, and welfare of workers employed in mines.
 
• The Act applies to all types of mines, including open-cast and underground mines, and lays down provisions for inspections, safety measures, and penalties for violations.
 
• It mandates the appointment of qualified managers and supervisors to oversee mining operations and ensure compliance with safety standards.
 
• The Act specifies working hours, conditions of employment, and provisions for the welfare of workers, including medical facilities, canteens, and sanitation.
 
• The Mines Act, 1952, is a crucial legislation aimed at improving the living and working conditions of miners, reducing workplace hazards, and preventing exploitation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The primary acts governing mining in India are:**

 
 
• The Mines Act, 1952, focusing on health, safety, and working conditions.
 
• The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act), which regulates the development and control of minerals under Union control, alongside specific rules like the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development & Regulation) Act, 2002 for offshore operations.
 
• These foundational laws, supplemented by various rules and amendments (like the MMDR Amendment Acts of 1986, 1994, 2010), create the framework for India's mining sector.

questions.question: Which type of Indian cinema refers to commercial, mainstream films primarily produced in Hindi, known for their songs, drama and spectacle?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Bollywood refers to the Indian Hindi-language film industry, primarily based in Mumbai (formerly Bombay), Maharashtra.
 
• It is widely recognized for its commercial, mainstream cinema featuring elaborate song-and-dance sequences, melodramatic narratives, and larger-than-life spectacle.
 
• Bollywood produces a significant portion of India's films and is one of the largest centers of film production globally.
 
• It is known for its unique blend of genres, including romance, action, comedy, drama, and musicals, often catering to mass audiences.
 
• Popular Bollywood movies often incorporate cultural elements, traditional music, and themes that resonate with Indian audiences, making it a cultural phenomenon worldwide.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indie films:**

 
 
• Indie films, or independent films, are produced outside the major studio system and often have a lower budget.
 
• They focus on artistic expression, unique storytelling, and niche audiences rather than commercial appeal.
 
• These films are known for their creative freedom and often explore unconventional themes or experimental filmmaking techniques.
 
 
 
• **Regional cinema:**
 
 
• Regional cinema refers to films made in various languages and regions of India, such as Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Bengali, Punjabi, Marathi, and others.
 
• These films often focus on regional culture, traditions, and local issues, catering to specific linguistic or cultural audiences.
 
• Regional cinema plays a significant role in showcasing India's diversity and has gained international recognition for its quality and storytelling.
 
 
 
• **Parallel cinema:**
 
 
• Parallel cinema, also known as art cinema, is a movement in Indian cinema characterized by realistic and issue-based storytelling.
 
• It emerged in the 1950s as an alternative to the commercial film industry, focusing on social and political themes.
 
• Directors like Satyajit Ray, Ritwik Ghatak, and Mrinal Sen were pioneers of this genre, emphasizing artistic and intellectual filmmaking over mass entertainment.

questions.question: The infamous Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred when Gandhi called all the Indians to observe April 6, 1919, as a day of non-violent protest against which of the following colonial policies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rowlatt Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Rowlatt Act, passed in March 1919, was officially called the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919.
 
• The act authorized the British government to imprison individuals suspected of revolutionary activities without trial for up to two years.
 
• This act sparked widespread anger and protests among Indians, as it curtailed civil liberties and judicial rights.
 
• In response, Mahatma Gandhi initiated the nationwide Satyagraha movement and called for April 6, 1919, to be observed as a day of non-violent protest.
 
• The infamous Jallianwala Bagh massacre on April 13, 1919, was a direct consequence of protests against the Rowlatt Act.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Partition of Bengal:**

 
 
• The Partition of Bengal took place in 1905 during the tenure of Lord Curzon, dividing Bengal into East Bengal and West Bengal.
 
• It was primarily justified by the British as an administrative measure but was widely seen as an attempt to divide Hindus and Muslims to weaken nationalist movements.
 
• The partition led to widespread protests and was eventually annulled in 1911.
 
 
 
• **Simon Commission:**
 
 
• The Simon Commission was a group of seven British MPs sent to India in 1928 to study constitutional reforms.
 
• It was widely opposed by Indians because it had no Indian representation, leading to protests and slogans like "Simon Go Back."
 
• Notably, Lala Lajpat Rai was injured during a protest against the Simon Commission and later succumbed to his injuries.
 
 
 
• **Minto-Morley Reforms:**
 
 
• The Minto-Morley Reforms were introduced in 1909 and aimed to provide limited political representation to Indians.
 
• It introduced separate electorates for Muslims, which sowed seeds of communalism in Indian politics.
 
• The reforms were criticized for being insufficient to meet the demands of Indian nationalists.

questions.question: What does the Constitution of India stipulate regarding the composition of the Election Commission of India (ECI)?

options.text: It is constitutionally fixed as a single-member body headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) only.
It must always be a three-member body (one Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners).
It must include one Election Commissioner from each major state to ensure federal balance
It may be single or multi-member; initially, there was only a Chief Election Commissioner until 1989.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It may be single or multi-member; initially, there was only a Chief Election Commissioner until 1989**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Constitution of India under Article 324 establishes the Election Commission of India (ECI) and grants it authority over the conduct of elections in India.
 
• Article 324 does not specify a fixed composition for the Election Commission; it gives the President of India the discretion to determine whether the ECI is a single-member or multi-member body.
 
• Initially, the ECI was a single-member body with only a Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) until 1989.
 
• In 1989, the ECI became a multi-member body with the appointment of two Election Commissioners in addition to the CEC. Since then, it has functioned as a three-member body in most instances.
 
• The President has the authority to appoint Election Commissioners, and the composition of the Election Commission may vary over time as per requirements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Election Commission of India (ECI) is a constitutional body established under Article 324 of the Constitution of India.

It is responsible for conducting free and fair elections to the Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.

 
• The ECI operates independently and is vested with powers to ensure impartiality and transparency in the electoral process.

questions.question: Which of the following leaders is associated with the concept of ‘Drain of Wealth’ theory?

• Dadabhai Naoroji is known as the **Grand Old Man of India** and was a key figure in Indian nationalism.
 
• He introduced the **'Drain of Wealth' theory**, which explained how the British colonial rule was draining economic resources from India.
 
• The theory was first articulated in his book **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India."**
 
• Naoroji argued that British policies led to a systematic transfer of India's wealth to Britain, causing widespread poverty in India.
 
• He highlighted factors like excessive land revenue, high taxation, and the export of raw materials without adequate compensation to India as contributors to the economic drain.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was also the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament and used his position to advocate for Indian interests.

• He is famous for his slogan **"Give me blood, and I will give you freedom."**
 
• Although he played a critical role in the freedom struggle.
 
 
 
• **MG Ranade:**
 
 
• Mahadev Govind Ranade was a noted social reformer and economist during the British rule.
 
• He emphasized industrialization and modern education as solutions for India’s economic challenges.
 
• While his contributions to Indian economics are significant.

questions.question: As per the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways of the Government of India, which port is known as the largest container port in India (as of May 2025)?
